course_title: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide
chapter_title: Defining Reliability: SLAs, SLOs, and SLIs
chapter_summary:
In the realm of distributed systems, reliability is not just a vague concept; it's a quantifiable attribute defined by a set of precise metrics and agreements. As system designers, we must move beyond simply saying a system is "reliable" and instead articulate *how* reliable it is, *what* we aim for, and *what* we promise to our users or customers. This is where Service Level Indicators (SLIs), Service Level Objectives (SLOs), and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) come into play. These three terms form a hierarchy, each building upon the last to provide a comprehensive framework for managing system performance and user expectations.

At the foundational level, we have **Service Level Indicators (SLIs)**. An SLI is a carefully chosen quantitative measure of some aspect of the service provided. It's the raw data point that tells us how our system is performing from the user's perspective. Think of SLIs as the "what to measure." Common examples include latency (the time it takes for a service to respond to a request), throughput (the number of requests processed per unit of time), error rate (the percentage of requests that result in an error), and availability (the percentage of time a service is operational and responsive). When selecting SLIs, it's crucial to pick metrics that directly reflect user experience and are measurable consistently. For instance, if you're designing an e-commerce platform, the latency for adding an item to a cart or completing a purchase would be a critical SLI, far more relevant than, say, the CPU utilization of a backend server if that server's performance doesn't directly impact user-facing response times. The key is to focus on user-centric metrics.

Building upon SLIs, we define **Service Level Objectives (SLOs)**. An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI, measured over a specific period. It's the "what we aim for." For example, if our SLI is "request latency for API X," an SLO might be "99% of API X requests must complete within 200 milliseconds over a 30-day rolling window." SLOs are internal targets that guide engineering teams. They help prioritize work, identify areas for improvement, and define what constitutes acceptable performance. Setting SLOs requires a deep understanding of the system's capabilities, its dependencies, and user expectations. If an SLO is too ambitious, teams might burn out trying to achieve an impossible target. If it's too lax, the system might degrade without anyone noticing. A well-defined SLO provides a clear signal when the system is underperforming and helps prevent minor issues from escalating into major outages. It also establishes a shared understanding of success within the engineering organization.

Finally, at the top of the hierarchy, we have **Service Level Agreements (SLAs)**. An SLA is a formal, legally binding contract between a service provider and a customer that specifies the minimum level of service the customer can expect. It's the "what we promise." SLAs are typically built around one or more SLOs and often include penalties or remedies if the agreed-upon service levels are not met. For example, an SLA might state that "the service will maintain 99.9% availability, and if this is not met in any given month, the customer will receive a 10% service credit." SLAs are critical for managing customer expectations and providing a framework for accountability. From a system design perspective, understanding the SLAs your system needs to support is paramount, as they directly influence architectural decisions regarding redundancy, disaster recovery, and operational procedures. Failing to meet an SLA can have significant financial and reputational consequences. Therefore, designing a system with the target SLAs in mind from the outset is far more effective than trying to bolt on reliability after the fact.

A common mistake in system design is to conflate these terms or to set unrealistic expectations. For instance, aiming for "five nines" (99.999%) availability for every single component of a system might be prohibitively expensive and unnecessary if the user experience doesn't demand it. Instead, a more nuanced approach involves identifying critical user journeys and setting appropriate SLIs and SLOs for those specific paths, potentially with different targets for less critical components. Another pitfall is to define SLIs that are too low-level or internal, such as CPU usage, without correlating them to actual user impact. While internal metrics are valuable for debugging, they don't directly measure service quality from the user's perspective. Always strive for user-centric SLIs.

When designing a system, consider how you will measure these SLIs. This often involves integrating monitoring tools that can collect metrics on latency, error rates, and throughput at various points in your system (e.g., load balancers, API gateways, individual microservices, database queries). For example, if you're designing a new API, you'd instrument its endpoints to report response times and error codes. These raw metrics then feed into dashboards and alerting systems that track your SLOs. If an SLO is breached, it triggers an alert, prompting the team to investigate and remediate. This proactive approach, driven by well-defined SLIs and SLOs, is the cornerstone of building and operating reliable distributed systems.

screens.title: Defining Reliability: SLAs, SLOs, and SLIs
screens.subtitle: A practical framework to quantify and promise service quality

narration.text: In this lesson we make reliability concrete. Rather than saying a system is "reliable," you will learn precise measures we use to observe, target, and promise quality: SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs. SLIs are the raw, user-centered signals — like latency or error rate — that tell us what users actually experience. SLOs are the engineering targets we set over time, for example a rolling 30-day latency target. SLAs are the external promises or contracts built from those targets that define remedies when service falls short. You will see why choosing user-centric SLIs matters, how to set realistic SLOs that avoid burnout, and why SLAs must be designed with architecture and cost in mind. I will also walk you through a concrete scenario for an authentication service so you can practice picking SLIs and SLOs, and we’ll discuss common mistakes teams make when they confuse internal health metrics with user impact. By the end you’ll be able to map user journeys to measurable signals and translate internal goals into customer commitments.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: SLIs measure user experience, SLOs set targets for those SLIs, and SLAs are customer-facing contracts built from SLOs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you will learn four core skills that make reliability actionable. First, you will be able to differentiate SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs and explain how they relate to each other. You’ll practice naming SLIs that reflect real user experience, such as latency for a checkout flow or error rate during login. Second, you will understand why SLOs are internal targets and how to choose measurement windows and realistic targets that guide engineering trade-offs without causing exhaustion. Third, you will learn how to instrument services so SLIs can be measured reliably in production and feed alerts when SLOs are breached. I’ll show a simple measurement pattern and a hands-on starter for an authentication service. Finally, you will recognize the operational and contractual implications of SLAs and how to convert internal SLOs into external commitments with appropriate error budgets. These skills let you design systems that are observable, measurable, and aligned with customer expectations.

keyIdea.text: Differentiate metrics, choose and measure SLIs, set SLOs, and translate them into SLAs safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.subtitle: Targets, measurement windows, and operational consequences

narration.text: In this continuation we'll focus on practical decision-making. You will learn how to pick measurement windows for SLOs — for example short windows for latency-sensitive paths and longer windows for availability trends — and why the choice affects alert noise and incident response. You will practice converting SLO violations into an operational response plan, including how an error budget is consumed and how teams prioritize reliability work versus feature development. You will also examine the consequences of missing SLAs: financial penalties, reputation damage, and the architectural decisions needed to meet stringent contracts. Finally, you will learn common mistakes to avoid, such as measuring low-level system metrics that are poorly correlated with user experience or setting uniformly extreme availability targets for all components. These skills help you design pragmatic, measurable reliability targets that guide engineering trade-offs.

keyIdea.title: Practical focus
keyIdea.text: Measurement windows, error budgets, and realistic SLOs help balance reliability work with feature velocity and cost.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Learning Objectives
Measurement windows & error budgets
  • Short windows (minutes to hours) catch transient latency spikes but can cause noisy alerts.
  • Long windows (days to months) smooth trends for availability planning and SLA reconciliation.
  • Error budget = allowed fraction of failures under the SLO; it informs prioritization between reliability and features.
  • Use different windows per user journey; not every component needs the same SLO strictness.
Operational consequences
SLAs expose you to customer remedies and must be reflected in architecture and runbooks. When planning, consider redundancy, failover, and recovery times aligned to contractual promises.
Common mistakes
  • Measuring CPU or memory as an SLI without mapping to user impact.
  • Setting identical five-nines targets for every component; cost is often disproportionate.
  • Ignoring measurement fidelity: if you can’t measure it consistently, you can’t operate to it.

screens.title: Service Level Indicator (SLI)
screens.subtitle: What to measure about your service

narration.text: A Service Level Indicator, or SLI, is a quantitative measure that captures an aspect of service quality from the user's perspective. An SLI should be directly tied to a user journey, measurable consistently, and sensitive to failures that users notice. Typical SLIs include latency for a specific A P I call, error rate for a user-facing endpoint, throughput for a critical operation, or availability defined as the percentage of successful requests over a window. For example, for an e-commerce checkout flow you might define an SLI as the fraction of checkout requests that complete without an error and under 500 milliseconds. A common misconception is to use low-level host metrics like C P U or disk input and output as SLIs; while useful for diagnostics, they don’t necessarily map to user experience. When choosing SLIs, prefer end-to-end measurements at the gateway or edge where possible. Also document how the metric is computed: what counts as a request, what errors are included, and how you handle retries or background processing. This clarity ensures that the SLI is reliable, actionable, and comparable over time. How would you define an SLI for a login that reflects real user impact?

keyIdea.title: SLI in one line
keyIdea.text: A measurable, user-focused signal that represents service quality for a specific user journey.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Service Level Indicator (SLI)
Definition
An SLI is a precise numeric measurement that reflects user-visible behavior. It must be consistently measurable and directly tied to a user journey.
How to choose an SLI
  • Pick user-centric events: API responses, checkout success, login completion.
  • Define inclusions/exclusions: which status codes or retries count as success.
  • Prefer edge or gateway measurements for end-to-end visibility.
Concrete example
SLI: Fraction of login requests completing with 200 OK within 300 ms, measured at the API gateway, counting first attempt only.
Why not internal metrics?

CPU or memory usage are important for operations but they don’t directly say whether a user could complete a purchase or sign in, so they are poor SLIs alone. Use them for diagnostics but not as primary service quality indicators.

Key Takeaway

SLIs must map to user impact and be computed consistently so teams can trust alerts and decisions driven by them.

Check your understanding

Name one SLI for an image upload feature and state what counts as success.

screens.title: Common SLI Types
screens.subtitle: Latency, Availability, Error Rate, Throughput — what they reveal

narration.text: SLIs come in a few common flavors, each revealing a different facet of user experience. Latency measures how long an operation takes and is crucial for interactive paths like search or login. Availability measures the fraction of time the service can respond to requests successfully, often expressed in percentage or "nines." Error rate is the proportion of requests that return failures, which directly signals correctness and reliability. Throughput measures capacity — how many requests or operations the system can process per unit time. A concrete example: for an A P I endpoint, latency tells you how snappy the endpoint feels, error rate tells you whether users get successful responses, throughput tells you whether the system can handle peak traffic, and availability aggregates success across many requests over time. A common misconception is to treat these metrics as interchangeable; they are complementary. A low error rate with very high latency still produces a poor user experience. Equally, high throughput with uncontrolled latency can consume capacity without delivering value. When you monitor these SLIs together they provide a fuller picture and help prioritize where to invest engineering effort.

keyIdea.title: SLI types
keyIdea.text: Use latency, availability, error rate, and throughput together to understand performance, correctness, capacity, and uptime.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Common SLI Types
Latency
Measure response time for a user action. Example: 95th percentile API response time for search must be under 200 ms.
Availability
Percentage of successful responses over a window, often used for SLAs (e.g., 99.9% availability).
Error Rate
Fraction of requests that fail. Example: HTTP 5xx or domain-specific failures affecting an operation.
Throughput
Requests processed per second or operations per minute. Use it to dimension capacity and discover saturation points.
Concrete scenario
An image-upload endpoint might have: throughput capacity of 200 uploads/sec, latency SLI of 95% under 600 ms, and error rate under 0.1%. Monitoring all three helps decide whether to scale, optimize code paths, or investigate failures.
Misconception
High throughput does not guarantee good latency or low error rate. Evaluate multiple SLIs before recommending remediation.

narration.text: A Service Level Objective is an explicit target or range applied to an SLI over a defined period. It answers the question: what performance do we aim to deliver? For example, an SLO could be "99% of A P I X requests complete within 200 milliseconds over a 30-day rolling window." SLOs guide engineering priorities: they inform alerting thresholds, drive capacity planning, and create a shared notion of acceptable quality. Setting SLOs involves understanding user expectations and system capabilities. If you set targets that are too ambitious, engineering teams may burn out chasing unattainable metrics; too lax and degradations go unnoticed. Choose measurement windows deliberately — short windows focus on immediate responsiveness, while longer windows provide stability for availability targets. Also decide how you treat retries and partial failures in your SLO definition. A typical misconception is to equate SLOs with SLAs; SLOs are internal and actionable, whereas SLAs are customer-facing. Finally, SLOs enable error budgets, which quantify the allowed distance from perfection and help teams balance feature work against reliability improvements. Service Level Objective (SLO) means an slo is a clear, measurable target for an sli over a time window that guides engineering action.. In practical terms, setting targets for slis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SLO in one line
keyIdea.text: An SLO is a clear, measurable target for an SLI over a time window that guides engineering action.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Service Level Objective (SLO)
What is an SLO?
An internal target on an SLI, defined with a value and a measurement window to drive alerts and prioritization.
Example
"99% of checkout requests succeed within 300 ms over a 30-day rolling window." This SLO shapes cadence for capacity and reliability work.
Decision points
  • Value: percentage or percentile you target (e.g., 99%, p95).
  • Window: rolling duration for evaluation (days, weeks, months).
  • Inclusions: what counts as a request and what responses are classified as success.
Why SLOs matter
They create actionable thresholds for alerts and help teams decide when to invest in reliability vs. new features by tracking error budgets tied to the SLO.
Misconception
An SLO is not an SLA. SLOs are internal guideposts; SLAs are promises that may include penalties if missed.
Key Takeaway

Set SLOs that reflect user expectations and system capability, and be explicit about measurement rules so responses are reliable.

screens.title: Choosing SLIs and Setting SLOs
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach based on user journeys

narration.text: Choosing SLIs and setting SLOs is a deliberate process that starts with identifying critical user journeys. Step one: map the top user flows that deliver business value — for example login, add-to-cart, and checkout in an e-commerce system. Step two: for each journey, pick one or two SLIs that capture success and responsiveness, such as success fraction and p95 latency for the checkout flow. Step three: choose an appropriate measurement window and target for each SLI. Short windows expose transient regressions; longer windows smooth variability and are appropriate for availability targets. Step four: define how to compute the SLI — what counts as success, how retries are handled, and where instrumentation occurs. Step five: set an SLO with an explicit error budget, then operationalize alerts and runbooks for SLO breaches. A common pitfall is to over-instrument every metric without prioritizing; instead, limit SLIs to those that directly impact users and that you will act on when they change. This process ensures your SLOs drive useful work and reduce firefighting on metrics that don't matter. Choosing SLIs and Setting SLOs means map user journeys → pick user-centric slis → choose windows & slos → define computation rules → operationalize error budgets.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach based on user journeys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Process summary
keyIdea.text: Map user journeys → pick user-centric SLIs → choose windows & SLOs → define computation rules → operationalize error budgets.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Choosing SLIs & Setting SLOs
Step 1 — Map journeys
List the critical user paths whose health matters most to the business.
Step 2 — Pick SLIs
Choose 1–2 SLIs per journey that reflect success and responsiveness.
Step 3 — Choose windows
Decide rolling windows for targets and alerting cadence.
Key Takeaway
Prioritize SLIs tied to user journeys and keep SLOs actionable so teams respond to real user impact.
Example: Checkout flow
SLI A: fraction of checkout requests that complete with an order confirmation. SLO A: 99% successful checkouts over a 30-day rolling window. SLIs B: p95 checkout latency & page load success.
Common mistake
Selecting too many SLIs dilutes focus. Limit to those you will act on and that represent critical user outcomes.
Check
For a login journey, what single SLI best represents user success and why?

screens.title: Error Budgets and Operational Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: How SLOs create room for change and prioritization

narration.text: An error budget quantifies how much unreliability your SLO allows. If an SLO requires 99.9% success over a period, the error budget is the remaining 0.1% of failures you can tolerate. This budget is a powerful planning tool: when you consume error budget, it signals that you should prioritize reliability work or slow down feature launches; when you have budget left, teams can safely ship new features. The error budget also helps avoid overreaction to small blips by framing them relative to the allowed budget. For example, a minor spike in latency that consumes a small fraction of the monthly error budget may warrant monitoring but not an immediate full-scale incident response. A common misconception is to treat error budgets as permission to be careless. Instead, use them intentionally to guide risk: create policies that define thresholds for automated actions, such as pausing risky deployments when a budget is nearly exhausted. Document how the budget is computed and how partial credits are handled. This practice aligns product, engineering, and operations around measurable tolerance for failure. Error Budgets and Operational Trade-offs means the allowed fraction of failures under an slo that teams can spend on changes before prioritizing reliability.. In practical terms, how slos create room for change and prioritization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error budget
keyIdea.text: The allowed fraction of failures under an SLO that teams can spend on changes before prioritizing reliability.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Error Budgets & Trade-offs
Definition
Error budget = 1 - SLO target (as a fraction) over the measurement window. It represents allowable unreliability.
Example calculation
If SLO is 99.9% availability for 30 days, error budget = 0.1% of that window. Teams track consumption via SLI measurements and plan accordingly.
Operational policy ideas
  • When 50% of budget is used: reduce risky deployments.
  • When 100% is exhausted: halt non-essential releases and prioritize fixes.
Why this helps teams
Error budgets give a measurable trade-off between innovation and reliability, enabling predictable governance decisions instead of ad hoc firefighting.
Misconception
An error budget is not a license to accept outages; it’s a planning tool for controlled risk and prioritization.
Check
How would you change deployment cadence when error budget is nearly exhausted for a critical user path?

screens.title: SLAs: Promises, Penalties, and Architecture
screens.subtitle: Why contractual commitments affect design decisions

narration.text: Service Level Agreements are formal commitments to customers that specify minimum service quality and often define remedies when the promise is broken. SLAs are typically expressed in terms of availability or other SLO-derived metrics, and they carry operational and financial implications. From an architecture perspective, accepting a strict SLA drives choices: added redundancy, multi-region failover, synchronous replication, and more aggressive disaster recovery plans. Each added reliability mechanism increases cost and complexity. A practical example: agreeing to 99.99% availability may force you to build cross-region failover and increased testing, whereas a 99.9% SLA might be achievable with single-region redundancy and robust recovery playbooks. A common pitfall is to sign SLAs before validating whether the system and runbooks can meet them. Always design with the SLA in mind — it determines acceptable risk and drives engineering investment. Also ensure measurement rules for the SLA are transparent so both parties understand what counts toward uptime and incidents. Treat SLAs as business decisions that must balance customer expectations, negotiable remedies, and architectural feasibility. SLAs: Promises, Penalties, and Architecture means an sla is a customer contract derived from slos that has legal or financial consequences and shapes architecture and operations.. In practical terms, why contractual commitments affect design decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SLA essence
keyIdea.text: An SLA is a customer contract derived from SLOs that has legal or financial consequences and shapes architecture and operations.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › SLAs & Architecture
What an SLA contains
Scope, measurable target (often availability), measurement window, reporting rules, and remedies or credits when missed.
Design implications
Strict SLAs usually require redundancy, failover, and verified recovery procedures. Each requirement increases cost and operational overhead.
Negotiation tip
Align SLA terms with achievable SLOs and document measurement details to avoid disputes about incidents and remedies.
Concrete contrast
A 99.9% SLA allows ~43 minutes of downtime per month; 99.99% allows ~4.3 minutes. These differences lead to dramatically different architecture and runbook investments.
Risk
Missing an SLA can incur credits or penalties and affects customer trust. Design SLAs with clear measurement rules and realistic architecture costs.
Key Takeaway

Treat SLAs as business-level constraints that should be matched by architecture and operational practice, not afterthoughts.

screens.title: Instrumentation & Measurement
screens.subtitle: How to collect SLIs reliably in production

narration.text: Measuring SLIs reliably requires consistent instrumentation at predictable system boundaries. A practical approach is to instrument at the A P I gateway or load balancer for end-to-end latency and success measurements, and inside services for more granular diagnostics. Your measurement plan should specify what counts as a request, which status codes are successes, and how retries or asynchronous work are treated. A simple instrumentation pattern is: record request start time, observe response code, classify success or failure, and emit a latency histogram and a success counter. These raw metrics then feed a time-series store and dashboards that evaluate SLOs over rolling windows. The chapter gives an example of using an aggregator like Prometheus to collect and compute percentiles and error rates. A common misconception is to sample inconsistently or change metric definitions over time; always version and document metrics so historical comparisons remain valid. Below is a conceptual code snippet showing how you might record latency and success at an endpoint. Instrumentation & Measurement means instrument at stable boundaries, define exact success criteria, and collect latency and success counters consistently.. In practical terms, how to collect slis reliably in production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Measurement rules
keyIdea.text: Instrument at stable boundaries, define exact success criteria, and collect latency and success counters consistently.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Instrumentation & Measurement
Measurement plan
  • Instrument at the gateway for end-to-end latency and success fraction.
  • Emit a histogram for latency and a counter for successes/failures.
  • Document the request and response criteria and any retry rules.
Collector note
Aggregate metrics in a time-series database and compute SLOs over rolling windows; this supports alerting and dashboards for on-call teams.
Conceptual instrumentation (pseudo-code)
// on request entry
start = timestamp()
// call handler
status, result = handleRequest(req)
latency_ms = timestamp() - start
// classify success (200-299)
is_success = (status >= 200 && status < 300)
emit_counter("requests_total", {"success": is_success ? "true" : "false"})
emit_histogram("request_latency_ms", latency_ms)
// prometheus-style aggregation then computes percentiles and error rate
Misconception
Changing metric definitions over time breaks trend comparisons. Version metrics and keep clear computation rules to ensure historical accuracy.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: Avoiding mistakes that undermine reliability efforts

narration.text: Teams often fall into predictable traps when defining and operating SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs. First, conflating internal metrics with user impact is common: C P U, memory, or disk may be useful internally, but they do not necessarily reflect whether a user can complete a task. Second, setting uniformly extreme targets for all components — for example, applying five nines everywhere — is expensive and often unnecessary; instead, prioritize critical user journeys. Third, inconsistent measurement rules or changing how success is computed over time make historical comparisons unreliable and reduce trust in alerts. Fourth, neglecting error budgets removes a governance mechanism that balances feature delivery against reliability work. Finally, signing SLAs without validating architecture and operational maturity can lead to penalties and emergency engineering work. For each pitfall, the remedy is straightforward: map metrics to user outcomes, tier components by criticality, document metric definitions, use error budgets with clear policies, and align SLAs with validated capability. These changes move teams from reactive firefighting to predictable reliability engineering. Common Pitfalls and Misconceptions means measure user impact, tier components, document metrics, use error budgets, and validate slas before committing.. In practical terms, avoiding mistakes that undermine reliability efforts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Measure user impact, tier components, document metrics, use error budgets, and validate SLAs before committing.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Pitfalls & Misconceptions
Pitfall: Internal metrics as SLIs
Remedy: Choose metrics that reflect user success and instrument at user-facing boundaries.
Pitfall: One-size-fits-all SLOs
Remedy: Tier components by criticality and set different SLOs for core journeys vs. helper services.
Pitfall: Changing metric definitions
Remedy: Version metrics, document computation details, and keep historical continuity for trend analysis.
Check
When reviewing your SLIs, ask whether each one maps to a user outcome and what action you will take when it breaches its SLO.
Key Takeaway

Clear definitions, tiering, and documented measurement rules are essential to trustworthy reliability practice.

screens.title: Hands-on: Authentication Service SLIs & SLOs
screens.subtitle: Define SLIs, propose SLOs, and plan measurement

narration.text: Now apply the concepts to a concrete service: user authentication. Start by choosing three critical SLIs: login request latency, successful login fraction, and password-reset success rate. For each SLI propose an SLO and a measurement window. For example, SLI: login latency; SLO: 99% of login requests complete under 300 ms over a 7-day rolling window. SLI: successful login fraction; SLO: 99.5% of first-attempt logins succeed over 30 days. SLI: password reset completion; SLO: 98% success within one hour over 30 days. Measurement strategy: instrument the login endpoint to emit latency histograms and success counters at the A P I gateway, aggregate with a time-series store such as Prometheus, and compute percentiles and error rates from those aggregates. Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Key Concepts
Service Level Indicator (SLI)
A measurable, user-focused metric such as latency, availability, error rate, or throughput.
Service Level Objective (SLO)
An internal target for an SLI over a measurement window that guides alerting and prioritization.
Service Level Agreement (SLA)
A customer-facing, often contractual commitment built from SLOs, with remedies for breaches.
Summary takeaway

Keep SLIs user-focused and measurable, set SLOs that balance ambition and cost, and let SLAs follow from validated SLOs and architecture.
